newsitem.title: USA: Pennzoil rejects hostile bid from Union Pacific.
newsitem.headline: Pennzoil rejects hostile bid from Union Pacific.

text.p: Pennzoil Co. on Tuesday formally rejected a $4.2 billion hostile takeover bid from Union Pacific Resources Group Inc. as inadequate, saying the company would deliver better value on its own.
Union Pacific vowed to continue its pursuit of Pennzoil.

Pennzoil Chairman James Pate said the company was now poised to take advantage of five years of restructuring and that its portfolio of assets, especially overseas, had already started to deliver value to shareholders.
"The board believes that the best interest of Pennzoil and its shareholders will be served by independently pursuing Pennzoil's strategic business plan rather than a sale of the company," Pate said.
He forecast that Pennzoil would match or beat Wall Street forecasts for the second quarter and full year and that Pennzoil's cash flow per share would rise to $12.50 this year from $9.50 in 1996.
"If you look at valuations for our peer group of six times cash flow, you will see that Pennzoil shares are trading at that level now, which is a sustainable level," said Pate.
Pennzoil shares closed down $1.125 at $75.375 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange before the bid was formally rejected.
Pate disputed that Union Pacific's cash and stock offer was worth $84 per share as Union Pacific has claimed, saying almost half of it is based on the value of Union Pacific shares.
Pate said the two-part offer, cash first for half the stock, was designed to tempt Pennzoil shareholders in so as to try to avoid getting Union Pacific shares in the second part of the offer.
There has been speculation that a "white knight" would emerge to save Pennzoil, but Pate scotched that talk.
"The best future for our company is as an independent company," he said.

However, Union Pacific said it would pursue Pennzoil, saying its offer was not only fair to all shareholders but offered better value than Pennzoil's current plans or what Pennzoil "predicts for four to five years from now".

Union Pacific said Pennzoil's board had allowed the company's stock price to slide 33 percent between the start of 1990 and the date the offer was made, during a time when the Dow Jones industrial average of leading U.S. shares had nearly tripled.

Union Pacific also said Pennzoil had squandered a $3.0 billion windfall which came as a result of a legal settlement with Texaco Inc. and that the money would have generated better returns in a passbook savings account.
Pennzoil said that part of the proceeds from that settlement had been invested in Chevron Corp. stock which was eventually used to purchase the overseas properties that Union Pacific coveted.
Pennzoil's Pate said production from one of its Caspian Sea projects with a potential 5 billion barrels of oil in reserves could start this fall.
Pennzoil also has a 30 percent stake in a consortium in the Karabakh field, also in the Caspian, which had a potential 1 billion to 2 billion barrels of oil reserves, he added.
